questionText: Listen to a financial aid officer briefing students on scholarship and loan options.
audioScript:
Situation: A financial aid officer addresses a group of new and returning students in a lecture hall to explain available funding options and application deadlines.
Officer: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Karen, the senior financial aid officer here at Northgate University. Today I'll walk you through the main types of financial support available.
Officer: First, merit-based scholarships. These are awarded to students with a grade point average of three point five or above. The application window opens on the first of March and closes on the fifteenth of April.
Student: Excuse me, is there a separate form for need-based grants?
Officer: Yes, indeed. Need-based grants require a separate application, and you must submit your family income statement. Grants range from five hundred to three thousand pounds per year.
Officer: We also offer work-study programmes. Students can work up to fifteen hours per week on campus and earn around nine pounds per hour. Positions are limited and assigned on a first-come, first-served basis.
Student: What about student loans?
Officer: Government loans are available to eligible students. Repayment begins six months after graduation, and the interest rate is currently two point five percent.
Officer: Finally, emergency bursaries are available for students facing unexpected financial hardship. You can apply at any time during the academic year by contacting the financial aid office directly.
Student: Where do we submit the applications?
Officer: All applications must be submitted online through the student portal. Paper applications are no longer accepted.

questionText: Listen to a careers advisor giving an overview of the upcoming internship fair.
audioScript:
Situation: A careers advisor briefs a group of second-year students about the annual internship fair, including logistics, preparation tips, and participating employers.
Advisor: Welcome, everyone. I'm Daniel, one of the careers advisors at Maple University. The annual internship fair is coming up next Friday in the Grand Hall.
Advisor: Over forty employers will attend, ranging from technology firms to non-profit organisations. The fair runs from ten in the morning until four in the afternoon.
Student: Do we need to register in advance?
Advisor: Yes, registration is compulsory. You must sign up through the careers portal by Wednesday at the latest. Walk-ins will not be admitted.
Student: What should we bring with us?
Advisor: Bring at least ten copies of your updated CV. There is also a CV clinic running on Tuesday afternoon in the careers centre if you need help polishing it.
Advisor: Dress code is smart business attire. Jeans and trainers are not permitted. First impressions matter.
Student: Are there any specific employers we should target?
Advisor: That depends on your field. For engineering students, I'd highlight Hartwell Engineering and BlueSky Robotics. For business students, Meridian Bank and Crestwood Consulting are actively recruiting.
Student: Will there be on-the-spot interviews?
Advisor: Some employers conduct brief screening interviews lasting about ten minutes. Prepare a short pitch about yourself and be ready to discuss your skills and experience.
Advisor: After the fair, follow up with a thank-you email to any recruiters you spoke with. This is a small but effective step.

questionText: Listen to an officer introducing the student union and its services.
audioScript:
Situation: A student union officer addresses a group of first-year students to introduce the union's structure, services, and how to get involved.
Officer: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Greenfield University. I'm Olivia, the vice president of the student union. I'm here to give you a quick introduction to who we are and what we do.
Officer: The student union is an independent body run by elected student officers. We represent your interests to the university and provide a range of services.
Student: How is the union structured?
Officer: We have a president, a vice president, and five part-time officers, each responsible for a specific area such as welfare, education, and sports. Elections are held every spring.
Student: What services does the union provide?
Officer: We run the advice centre, which offers free and confidential support on housing, academic appeals, and welfare issues. It's open Monday to Friday, ten to four.
Officer: We also manage over sixty student societies, from debate to drama to photography. The society sign-up fair takes place during freshers' week on the main lawn.
Student: How can we join the union?
Officer: All registered students are automatically members, free of charge. To get involved in running things, you can attend our weekly general meetings on Wednesdays at six in the union building.
Officer: We also publish a monthly newsletter called The Student Voice. You can subscribe on our website to stay updated on events and campaigns.
Student: Can we suggest new initiatives?
Officer: Absolutely. You can submit proposals through our online portal. If they gather enough support, they'll be discussed at the next general meeting.

questionText: Listen to an IT services manager giving a tour of the campus technology facilities.
audioScript:
Situation: An IT services manager guides a group of new students through the campus technology centre, explaining available computing resources and support.
Manager: Welcome to the Whitfield Technology Centre. I'm Marcus, the IT services manager. I'll be showing you around our main computing facilities today.
Manager: This building houses four computer labs, each with forty workstations. Labs A and B are on the ground floor and are open twenty-four hours a day. Labs C and D are upstairs and close at ten p.m.
Student: Do we need a special account to log in?
Manager: You use your standard university username and password. Your account gives you access to all campus software, including specialist packages like statistical analysis tools and design software.
Student: Is there wireless internet across campus?
Manager: Yes, Wi-Fi is available in all buildings. The network is called CampusNet. You connect once using your university credentials, and it will remember your device automatically.
Manager: For printing, we use a follow-me system. You send your document to any printer, then tap your student card at the device to release it. Colour printing costs fifteen pence per page.
Student: What if we have technical problems?
Manager: The IT help desk is on the ground floor, open from eight a.m. until eight p.m. on weekdays. You can also submit tickets online at any time, and we aim to respond within four working hours.
Manager: Finally, all students get one terabyte of cloud storage through the university system. You can sync files across your devices and access them anywhere.

questionText: Listen to a coordinator explaining the disability services available at the university.
audioScript:
Situation: A disability services coordinator addresses a group of students and staff to outline the support available for students with disabilities and the process for requesting accommodations.
Coordinator: Good afternoon. I'm Dr. Fiona Hughes, the disability services coordinator at Ashworth University. I'd like to explain what we offer and how to access support.
Coordinator: Our office supports students with a wide range of conditions, including physical disabilities, sensory impairments, learning difficulties such as dyslexia, and long-term health conditions.
Student: How do we register with the service?
Coordinator: You begin by completing an online registration form on our portal. You'll also need to provide evidence of your condition, such as a medical letter or an educational psychologist's report.
Student: What kind of accommodations are available?
Coordinator: Common accommodations include extra time in exams, usually twenty-five percent additional time, note-taking support, and accessible seating in lecture halls. We can also arrange sign language interpreters upon request.
Coordinator: For students with visual impairments, we provide materials in alternative formats, including large print and braille. Audio recordings of lectures can also be arranged with the lecturer's permission.
Student: Is there dedicated study space?
Coordinator: Yes, we have two assistive technology rooms on the second floor of the library. Each is equipped with screen-reading software, ergonomic chairs, and adjustable desks. They can be booked up to a week in advance.
Coordinator: Our office is located in the Student Services Building, room one-oh-seven. We operate on an appointment basis, available Monday through Friday, nine to five.
Student: Is there a deadline to request exam accommodations?
Coordinator: Yes, exam accommodation requests must be submitted at least four weeks before the exam date. Late requests may not be processed in time.

questionText: Listen to a counsellor introducing the university's counselling services to new students.
audioScript:
Situation: A senior counsellor speaks to a group of new students during orientation week to introduce the university's mental health and wellbeing services, including how to book appointments and what to expect.
Counsellor: Welcome, everyone. I'm Dr. James Whitfield, a senior counsellor at the Wellbeing Centre. I want to tell you about the counselling services available to all registered students at this university.
Counsellor: The Wellbeing Centre offers free and confidential counselling to every enrolled student. There is no charge, and nothing is shared with your academic department without your explicit consent.
Student: What types of issues can we bring to counselling?
Counsellor: Students come to us for a wide range of reasons, including anxiety, depression, homesickness, relationship difficulties, and stress related to academic pressure. No concern is too small.
Student: How do we book an appointment?
Counsellor: You can self-refer through our online portal. After submitting the form, you'll be offered an initial assessment within five working days. This first session is a conversation to understand your needs and recommend the right support.
Counsellor: Following the assessment, you may be offered short-term counselling, typically six to eight weekly sessions of fifty minutes each. If longer-term support is needed, we can refer you to external services.
Student: Do you offer any group sessions?
Counsellor: Yes. We run workshops on managing exam stress, building resilience, and mindfulness. These are held every Thursday afternoon in the seminar room and no registration is required.
Student: What should I do in a crisis outside of office hours?
Counsellor: If you experience a mental health crisis when the centre is closed, you should call the twenty-four-hour crisis line. The number is on the back of your student card. Alternatively, you can go directly to the nearest hospital emergency department.
Counsellor: Our centre is located in the East Wing of the Health Building. We're open Monday to Friday, nine a.m. to six p.m. Please don't hesitate to reach out, even if you're unsure whether counselling is right for you.

questionText: Listen to an academic officer briefing students on the university's academic integrity policies.
audioScript:
Situation: An academic integrity officer addresses a group of first-year postgraduate students to explain plagiarism, collusion, the penalties for academic misconduct, and how to avoid violations.
Officer: Good morning. I'm Professor Eleanor Bryant, the academic integrity officer at Kingsford University. This session is compulsory for all new postgraduate students, so please listen carefully.
Officer: Academic integrity means honesty and responsibility in all academic work. The three most common breaches are plagiarism, collusion, and contract cheating.
Student: Could you explain the difference between plagiarism and collusion?
Officer: Certainly. Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own without proper acknowledgment. Collusion is when two or more students work together on an assignment that is meant to be completed individually.
Officer: Contract cheating is the most serious offence. This involves paying a third party, such as an essay mill, to produce work on your behalf. The minimum penalty for contract cheating is immediate expulsion from the university.
Student: What are the penalties for plagiarism?
Officer: Penalties depend on severity. For a first offence of minor plagiarism, the typical penalty is a mark of zero for the assignment and a mandatory training module. For repeat or serious offences, penalties can include failing the entire module or suspension.
Student: How can we avoid plagiarism?
Officer: Always cite your sources using the required referencing style. We use the Harvard system across most departments. Quotation marks must be used for direct quotes, and paraphrased ideas still require a citation.
Officer: All written submissions are checked through Turnitin, a similarity detection software. You will see a similarity score, but there is no fixed percentage that automatically triggers a penalty. Each case is reviewed individually by a panel.
Student: Can we work with classmates on homework?
Officer: Group discussion is encouraged, but unless your tutor explicitly permits collaborative submission, each student must write up their own answers independently. When in doubt, ask your tutor for clarification.
